subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: Find the sum of the infinite series 1 + 1/3 + (1·3)/(3·6) + (1·3·5)/(3·6·9) + … ∞.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.32 — LAQ chapter 3 Binomial Theorem, answer 26.1. Printed appearances: TS 15. THE 2+1+2+1+1 SPLIT IS THE BOOK'S SHAPE: answer 27 on book p.33 prints [2 Marks] against rewriting the series with factorials, [1 Mark] against the comparison with the standard expansion, [2 Marks] against finding p, q and x, [1 Mark] against evaluating the power, and [1 Mark] against the final line. recall_prompt: Say how you would find the sum of this series — how you rewrite it, what you compare it with, how you find p, q and x, and what the sum comes to.
insider_note: The marks are for matching p, q and x, and x is not the common ratio: the bracket holds x/q, so x = 2/3, not 1/3. The answer stays as √3 — a decimal is not the expected final form.

steps.label: Rewrite with factorials
steps.margin_note: First two marks. Each denominator is a product like 5·10·15 = 5³·(1·2·3), so every term becomes (a product)/(k!) times (1/3)ᵏ. This series already starts with 1 and 1/3, so nothing has to be added.

recall.must_convey: That the series is rewritten so the k-th term is a product over k! times (1/3) to the power k.
accept: write each term as a product over k factorial times one by three to the power k
split each denominator into three to the power k times k factorial
bring the series to the shape one plus p by one factorial into x by q and so on
prathi term ni k factorial tho, one by three power k tho rayali
rewrite the denominators as powers of three times factorials

steps.why: The standard expansion of (1 − x)^(−p/q) has a k! in every denominator and a fixed ratio x/q raised to k. Until the given series is written in that exact shape, p, q and x cannot be read off.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to add the missing terms on both sides when the series starts late, so the comparison has no 1 to match.
Writing 5·10·15 as 5·3! instead of 5³·3! — every factor carries a 3.
Losing the alternating sign when the terms alternate.

steps.label: Compare with the standard expansion
steps.margin_note: Third mark, for WRITING the standard expansion beside the series. The examiner looks for the pattern p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q) over 1!, 2!, 3!. All plus signs mean the (1 − x) form.

recall.must_convey: That the series is compared with the expansion of (1 − x) to the power minus p by q, whose coefficients are p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q) over 1!, 2!, 3!.
accept: compare with the expansion of (1 − x) to the power minus p by q
match it with one plus p by one factorial into x by q plus p into p plus q by two factorial into x by q squared and so on
use the standard binomial series with negative fractional index (1 − x) to the power minus p by q
(1 − x)^(−p/q) formula tho compare cheyali
the pattern p then p into p plus q over the factorials is the standard series

steps.why: This is the only binomial expansion whose coefficients grow as p, p(p + q), p(p + q)(p + 2q). Naming it turns the rest of the question into reading off three numbers.
common_mistakes: Using the (1 − x) form for an alternating series or the (1 + x) form for an all-plus series.
Writing p(p + 1) instead of p(p + q) — the step between factors is q, not 1.

steps.label: Find p, q and x
steps.margin_note: Fourth and fifth marks. p is the first factor (1), p + q is the second (3) so q = 2, and x/q equals the common ratio 1/3 so x = q/3 = 2/3.

recall.must_convey: That p = 1 and p + q = 3 give q = 2, and x/q = 1/3 gives x = two by three.
accept: p is one, p plus q is three so q is two, and x by q is one by three so x is two by three
the first factor gives p equal to one and the second gives q equal to two
x by q equals one by three so x equals two by three
p one, q two vasthai, x by q one by three kabatti x two by three
read off p from the first numerator and q from the gap between the factors

steps.why: Three unknowns need three matches: the first numerator fixes p, the second fixes p + q, and the ratio inside the bracket fixes x/q. Nothing else in the series is free.
common_mistakes: Taking x = 1/3 directly — the bracket holds x/q, so x = q × 1/3.
Reading q from the second factor as a whole instead of as p + q.

steps.label: Evaluate the power
steps.margin_note: Sixth mark. Substitute p, q, x into (1 − x)^(−p/q) and simplify the fraction inside the bracket before touching the exponent.

recall.must_convey: That substituting gives one by three to the power minus half, which is three to the power half.
accept: substituting gives one by three to the power minus half, which is three to the power half
put the values into (1 − x)^(−p/q) and simplify to get one by three to the power minus half, which is three to the power half
the bracket becomes one by three and the power gives one by three to the power minus half, which is three to the power half
values substitute cheste one by three to the power minus half, which is three to the power half vasthundi
simplify the bracket first then apply the negative index
heard_as: one by three to the power minus half, which is three to the power half

steps.why: A negative index inverts the fraction and a fractional index takes a root. Doing the inversion first keeps the root over a simple fraction.
common_mistakes: Inverting the exponent instead of the fraction when the index is negative.
Leaving a root in the denominator without a clear final value.

steps.label: State the sum
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. 3 to the power half is √3 — write it as a root, not as a decimal.

recall.must_convey: That the sum of the series is √3.
accept: the sum is root three
S equals root three
three to the power half which is root three
sum root three vasthundi
the series adds up to root three

steps.why: The whole series reduces to one number because it IS the expansion of (1 − 2/3) to the power −1/2, which is √3.
common_mistakes: Stopping at (1/3) to the power −1/2 without simplifying.
